alt: Two overlapping ovals. Households share an address; families are linked by kinship. Single person and shared households are households but not families; a family living together is both; relatives who live apart, as in a modified extended family, are a family but not one household. Murdock’s 1949 definition is noted with its limits.
caption: A single person household is a household but not a family.

alt: A grid judging five family structures, nuclear, horizontal extended, beanpole, reconstituted and lone parent, from the position of children, women, older relatives and society, so that each strength or limitation says who gains or loses.
caption: Say who gains and who loses: that turns a point into a developed one.

alt: Three sources of diversity. Cross-cultural: the Nayar and the Israeli kibbutz challenge Murdock’s universal nuclear family. Social class: Young and Willmott’s Bethnal Green families lived near kin, while the mobile middle class keep a modified extended family. Ethnicity: South Asian joint families, adapting over generations.
caption: Family patterns vary with culture, class and ethnicity.

alt: The New Right see family diversity as a problem, with Murray linking lone parenthood to welfare and missing male role models. Postmodernists see it as choice, with Stacey’s divorce-extended family. A note explains Chester’s point that snapshot figures overstate diversity because most people pass through a nuclear family.
caption: Say which side each view takes on whether diversity is good.

alt: Types of marriage grouped by question. How is the partner chosen: arranged with consent, which is not forced marriage, or love marriage. What is the relationship like: an empty shell marriage stays together in name only. How many partners: monogamy, and serial monogamy, which can lead to a reconstituted family.
caption: Arranged is not forced; serial monogamy leads to reconstituted families.
